item.title: Ultracold cesium atoms reveal Bethe strings predicted nearly a century ago
item.description: In 1931, physicist Hans Bethe predicted that, in certain one-dimensional quantum systems, particles can bind together to form multi-particle states known as Bethe strings. Unlike ordinary molecules, which are held together by chemical bonds, Bethe strings arise purely from interactions between particles and exist only in one dimension. For decades, Bethe strings remained primarily a theoretical concept. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fighting poverty today may build concern for the people of tomorrow
item.description: Does helping people struggling to survive today make any difference for future generations? New research from the University of Utah has documented evidence that it does. Rather than viewing present-day poverty and long-term risks as competing priorities, the research team led by psychologist Kyle Fiore Law sees them as interconnected. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Bizarre galactic radio source remains active for two decades with no detectable X-rays
item.description: Astronomers have identified a peculiar radio transient in the Milky Way that has remained active for more than two decades, defying the behavior expected of known classes of galactic radio sources. The paper posted to the arXiv preprint server on Aug. 21 discusses the rare event that may have caused this bizarre radio emission. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Inspiration alone won't solve Australia's teacher shortage, study reveals
item.description: A $10 million Australian government campaign celebrating inspirational teachers risked overlooking the workplace conditions driving educators from the profession, according to new research led by Curtin University published in the Journal of Education Policy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Starfish program creates new jobs
item.description: In a win for people and the environment, new economic modeling from James Cook University researchers reveals that a $5 million investment to control crown-of-thorns (CoTS) starfish numbers in the Cairns region created 61 new jobs and generated $20 million in economic activity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En 1976, un becario de la NASA compró 1.150 cintas de la agencia por 200 dólares. 32 años después descubrió que lo que había en tres valía 1,82 millones
item.description: En 1976, Gary George pagó 217,77 dólares por unas 1.150 cintas magnéticas que la NASA había decidido liquidar como material excedente. Su plan era sencillo: venderlas a televisiones para que grabaran encima de ellas. Pero su padre reparó en las etiquetas de tres rollos y le aconsejó conservarlos. En ellas se podía leer: “APOLLO 11 EVA | July 20, 1969”. George tardaría décadas en descubrir exactamente qué había comprado . Un becario y las cintas de la NASA. Gary George era estudiante de ingeniería en la Universidad Lamar y había conseguido unas prácticas en el Johnson Space Center de la NASA… Fuente: Xataka.

item.description: As Africa prepares for the arrival of a powerful El Niño weather event, an international team of researchers led by the University of Sydney and Imperial College London has found that access to improved forecasts alone will not protect many of the region's poorest livestock farmers from the impacts of climate change. item.title: China’s self-powered neural device helps stroke survivors walk naturally
item.description: Scientists have developed a lightweight, battery-free device that could help improve the mobility of people with difficulty walking, such as stroke survivors. Developed by researchers in Hong Kong and mainland China, the neural prosthesis uses energy generated by the wearer’s own movements to electrically stimulate their muscles, helping to flex their ankle and restore their natural walking pattern. This could prevent falls for stroke survivors, elderly individuals, and others living with... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: ESA’s FLEX mission reveals the secret glow of plants
item.description: Video: 00:06:30 Plants may look still and silent, but every leaf is constantly responding to its environment. As plants photosynthesise, they emit an incredibly faint glow called fluorescence. Invisible to our eyes, this signal can reveal how plants are using sunlight and how they respond to heat, drought, pests and other environmental stresses. ESA’s Fluorescence Explorer, or FLEX, will detect this faint signal from space. Using its highly sensitive FLORIS instrument, FLEX will map plant fluorescence across Earth, giving scientists a new way to observe plant health and photosynthetic… Fuente: European Space Agency.

Fuente: European Space Agency.

item.title: Consumers demand transparency, but is it rewarded?
item.description: Transparent supply chains boost consumer trust—if the results are positive. But what if they aren't? A new paper by Kühne Logistics University (KLU), in collaboration with the University of Tennessee and Tilburg University, published in the Journal of Business Logistics, reaches a surprising conclusion. The researchers advise companies: It's better to publish mixed results than none at all. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: JWST ruled out finding tiny moons around an exoplanet—that's great news
item.description: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has opened many wonders of the cosmos to scientists since it began science operations a few years ago. But one thing it hasn't done is find an "exomoon." These still-theoretical moons orbit exoplanets in other star systems, and JWST was supposed to find a plethora of them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Palo Alto’s 500-foot horizontal levee reuses wastewater to restore marshes and test sea-rise defence
item.description: Palo Alto engineers have created a unique horizontal levee along Harbor Marsh. This innovative structure combines native plants and treated wastewater for coastal protection. The project aims to provide habitat and adapt shorelines to rising sea levels. Researchers are monitoring its performance as a pilot for future defenses. This living shoreline offers a new model for coastal resilience and ecosystem integration. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Astronomers unmask a supernova impostor
item.description: A distant star has captured astronomers' attention over the past decade, teasing them with indications that it will soon explode as a supernova. But new research shows that something else entirely is behind the star's outbursts. Rather than an impending catastrophic explosion, a previously unseen companion may be responsible for the star's behavior. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Masked tectonic structures suggest Mercury contracted 40% more than its visible scars alone indicate
item.description: The surface of Mercury is filled with craters, ridges and steep cliffs. Over billions of years, as the planet's interior cooled, the planet also shrank. Just as the skin of a drying fruit wrinkles when what is inside it shrinks, Mercury's rocky surface crumpled into ridges and cliffs as its interior cooled and the planet contracted. Mercury has quite literally grown smaller with age. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: AI automates 3D membrane mapping, matching manual results in a fraction of time
item.description: Cell membranes and the proteins within them control many vital processes and play a key role in health and disease. But studying them in 3D images of cells has so far meant slow, manual work. A team from Helmholtz Munich, the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and the Biozentrum of the University of Basel has developed MemBrain v2, an AI tool that automates this task—cutting work that once took weeks down to a few hours. The study is published in Nature Methods. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Luminescence dating pushes age of South Dakota's Mammoth Site back by more than 100,000 years
item.description: Deep within an ancient sinkhole lie the remains of dozens of mammoths, prehistoric wanderers who waded into the warm springs to their deaths. These deaths had long been accepted as having occurred roughly 26,000 years ago, but new dates published in the journal Quaternary Research suggest these ice-age giants were more than 160,000 years old. Fuente: Phys.org.

Sin embargo, a medida que cumplimos años, la ciencia nos advierte que este ciclo repetitivo puede afectar a la masa muscular de manera persistente. La fluctuación de peso. item.title: The tourism industry is slowly waking up to solo travelers' needs
item.description: Solo travel is surging—and an industry still largely built for two is taking note. Google reported in April 2026 that online searches involving "solo travel" hit an all-time high this year, with queries for "women solo travel" reaching a 15-year peak. Hilton's 2026 trends report found that 26% of travelers planned to take a trip alone this year and that nearly half said they planned to add solo days to the front or back of a family trip. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Gravitational-wave analysis narrows the search for black hole impostors
item.description: Black holes are regions of spacetime where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. When two black holes orbit each other and merge, they produce gravitational waves (i.e., ripples in spacetime) that can resemble those emitted by mergers involving other exotic compact objects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Fish may be highly sensitive to antidepressants found in water
item.description: Many of the drugs that target human brain chemistry, such as antidepressants, are still biologically active when they leave the body. These substances and their metabolites can persist in wastewater and eventually end up in the sea, rivers or other aquatic environments. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists find a new layer of Alzheimer’s hidden in the genome
item.description: Scientists found that the 3D organization of DNA is disrupted in several types of brain cells affected by Alzheimer’s disease, altering how important genes are switched on and off. The discovery reveals a previously underexplored layer of the disease that could open new paths for understanding and eventually treating Alzheimer’s. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Cataract surgery will be needed in space, surgeon predicts
item.description: An eye surgeon with a passion for space since childhood predicts that as astronauts start to make journeys to the moon and Mars in the near future, eye surgery in space will eventually become a necessity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicists can’t agree on how the Universe works
item.description: A massive worldwide survey of physicists has revealed surprisingly little agreement about some of the universe’s biggest mysteries. No majority backed the standard cosmological model, a leading explanation for dark matter, or any single theory of quantum gravity. One area of stronger agreement stood out: 68% said the Big Bang does not necessarily represent the beginning of time. Researchers say the divisions show just how alive and unsettled the frontiers of physics remain. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A 1,000-fold longer charge lifetime helps organic catalyst produce solar hydrogen faster
item.description: Researchers from the Ningbo Institute of Materials Technology and Engineering (NIMTE) of the Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS), in collaboration with researchers from the Technical Institute of Physics and Chemistry of CAS, have developed a coumarin-linked covalent organic framework (COF) that enables high-efficiency photocatalytic water splitting for hydrogen production. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's next great observatory could spot oceans on distant worlds
item.description: We've found more than 5,500 exoplanets so far. Dozens of them are in the habitable zones of their parent stars, where, at least in theory, they could host an ocean. But we've never definitively found a liquid ocean on another planet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Most men don’t know dairy is linked to prostate cancer risk
item.description: Most men may be missing an important dietary clue about prostate cancer. A new survey found that only 20% knew research has linked dairy consumption with increased prostate cancer risk, while 66% said they would consider avoiding dairy after learning about the connection. Studies have also associated plant-based diets with substantially lower risks of prostate cancer, progression, and recurrence. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Global warming is breaking a 400-year climate link between two oceans
item.description: The Indian and Pacific oceans have been climatically linked for centuries, but scientists say that connection is now breaking down in an exceptional way. Ancient climate records suggest volcanoes disrupted the relationship in the past, while today human-caused warming appears to be driving a much more unusual shift. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists are building a microscope powered by a quantum computer
item.description: Scientists are combining an electron microscope with a quantum computer to squeeze far more information from each electron. The approach could reveal faint details with fewer electrons, helping protect fragile samples that conventional microscopy can damage. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: China’s FAST telescope maps neutral hydrogen, the cosmic gas for making stars
item.description: China’s FAST telescope has compiled the world’s largest catalogue of neutral hydrogen beyond the Milky Way, replacing a long-dominant US survey as the main reference for mapping the gas that fuels the formation of stars and galaxies. The FAST All-Sky H I Survey (FASHI), conducted with the 500-metre (1,640-foot) radio dish in southwest China’s Guizhou province, released its second batch of data this week. It contains 156,411 extragalactic sources – nearly five times the number detected by the... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: Researchers pinpoint key early-universe measurement with record precision
item.description: An international team, including researchers from the University of Minnesota Twin Cities, has reached a major milestone in "precision cosmology" by measuring the amount of helium created in the universe's first five minutes with unprecedented accuracy. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA-backed scientists turn plastic waste into edible cookies
item.description: Scientists have engineered yeast to turn PET plastic and agricultural waste into ingredients for protein-rich, 3D-printed cookies called µBites. Developed partly for NASA’s Deep Space Food Challenge, the system can produce proteins, fats, vitamins, and even vanilla flavoring from waste materials. Researchers hope the unusual technology could eventually help address both plastic pollution and food insecurity, while also supplying food in extreme environments such as deep-space missions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Physicists discover a hidden “curveball” in quantum light
item.description: Researchers have experimentally demonstrated the optical Magnus effect for the first time, revealing that a tightly focused laser interacts most strongly with an atom slightly away from the beam’s center. The unexpected shift is similar to the physics that makes a spinning table tennis ball curve through the air. Because lasers are used to control qubits, the effect could create errors in quantum computers, but it might also provide a new way to couple qubits together. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Feather found in dinosaur poop may explain how birds survived the asteroid that killed dinosaurs
item.description: The 66-million-year-old feather found inside fossilised dinosaur poop may offer clues about why some birds survived the asteroid impact that killed most dinosaurs. Researchers found feathers, fish scales and bird bones in the coprolite. The feather’s primitive structure suggests insulation and moulting may have played a role in determining which birds survived. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: AI uncovers hidden Ozempic side effects across 400,000 Reddit posts
item.description: AI analysis of 400,000 Reddit posts found that users of drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, Mounjaro, and Zepbound reported unexpected symptoms including menstrual changes, chills, hot flashes, and fatigue. Researchers cannot say the medications caused these problems, but the patterns may reveal overlooked signals worth studying. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists used centuries-old aurora sightings: their method placed solar minima within 2 years with more than 90% reliability
item.description: Ancient auroras are unlocking secrets of solar activity, offering scientists a glimpse into the Sun's behavior long before our time. By employing a new statistical method to analyze historical sky observations, researchers have pieced together eight distinct cycles of solar activity from 1560 to 1640. This intriguing study correlates well with various independent solar records, enhancing our understanding of solar dynamics pre-dating contemporary measurements. Fuente: The Times of India - World.

item.title: Venus’s pale yellow clouds may hide something surprisingly dark
item.description: A century-old mystery in Venus’s clouds just became more intriguing, as scientists calculated how strongly the unidentified material behind its dark ultraviolet patterns must absorb light. The results sharply narrow the possibilities and could help future spacecraft determine whether the mysterious substance is organic, inorganic, or something unexpected. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists find water was fueling volcanoes 3 billion years ago
item.description: Ancient rocks from Western Australia suggest water was reaching deep inside Earth more than three billion years ago, long before modern plate tectonics may have fully developed. Researchers propose that water-rich pieces of crust periodically sank into the mantle through a process they call “dripduction.” The buried water then helped produce magma and volcanic eruptions. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: A hidden compound in healthy foods may worsen IBD
item.description: A natural compound found in foods such as spinach, almonds, and sweet potatoes may aggravate gut inflammation in people with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis because their intestines appear to handle it differently. Researchers say the finding could open the door to lower-oxalate diets or microbiome treatments tailored specifically to people with IBD. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Ozempic and Wegovy may raise hair loss risk in some men
item.description: GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic, Wegovy, and Zepbound may increase hair-loss risk by 7% in men who are already genetically susceptible to male-pattern baldness. The findings suggest thinning hair may not be caused only by rapid weight loss and could also reflect a biological link between GLP-1 activity and hair follicles. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Denisovan fossils in China reveal an ancient ‘hunting paradise’
item.description: Denisovan remains discovered in southwestern China reveal that Yunnan province’s warm, biodiverse plateau was a “hunting paradise” for the hominins during a global glacial period, according to new research published in the journal Nature. Within the region’s coniferous forests and forest-steppe environments, this archaic human group established a stable subsistence pattern highly adapted to local resources through specialised hunting and the intensive exploitation of animals. The extinct... Fuente: South China Morning Post.

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden switch that shuts down inflammation
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a natural braking system that helps the immune system switch off inflammation and prevent harmful immune cells from building up. Boosting this pathway in people reduced inflammation-related immune changes and sped up pain relief, pointing toward potential new treatments for chronic inflammatory diseases. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: AI could make holiday planning easier for overwhelmed travelers
item.description: Generative AI could help overwhelmed travelers organize their thoughts, compare options and complete vacation plans they might otherwise abandon, according to new research from the University of Surrey. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Japan's Hayabusa2 achieves first-ever laser ranging experiment with an asteroid
item.description: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency's (JAXA) Hayabusa2 spacecraft reached another milestone this summer, a first for space agencies. On Sunday, July 5, the probe conducted the first successful laser-ranging experiment during a flyby of asteroid Torifune, the first exploration target of Hayabusa2's Extended Mission. This latest milestone will advance the capabilities of JAXA and other space agencies as they pursue future missions involving near-Earth asteroids (NEAs) and other deep-space objects. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A brief history of the hangover and its remedies—from cabbages to cloves and the lungs of a goat
item.description: Anyone who has ever woken up with a hangover will recognize its physical and psychological effects: headache, nausea, self-loathing, regret and perhaps even some shame at the uninhibited behavior that accompanied the intoxication. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Unified framework shows thermoelectric performance depends on more than the material itself
item.description: Thermoelectric materials can directly convert heat into electricity, making them promising for recovering waste heat from factories, vehicles and other sources. They can also transport heat when an electric current is applied through a phenomenon known as the Peltier effect. These properties have attracted considerable interest in energy-saving technologies and thermal management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Silicon nanosphere coatings deliver glossy, nonfading color on 3D surfaces
item.description: "Color coatings are expected to provide vivid color, brightness, gloss and long-term durability, yet no existing technology satisfies all of these requirements simultaneously," says Kobe University materials engineer Hiroshi Sugimoto. Conventional coatings usually rely on relatively thick pigment layers that fade and add significant weight. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En 1997 liberaron 1.541 alces en unas viejas minas de carbón a cielo abierto. 30 años después, hay una manada de 13.000
item.description: Hubo un tiempo en el que los alces (orientales) desaparecieron por completo de Kentucky: el último fue tiroteado en Pensilvania el 1 de septiembre de 1877, como recogen registros históricos . Precisamente la caza y la pérdida de su hábitat acabaron con la especie , que durante más de un siglo dejó de verse por los Apalaches. En 1997, el estado de Kentucky inició un ambicioso programa de reintroducción de alces y pasó algo altamente improbable: la nueva manada de alces se desbordó y dio un "bombazo" genético. El alce vuelve por todo lo alto . Como explica el Departamento de Recursos de Pesca y… Fuente: Xataka.

item.title: Deer Learn To Ignore Deterrents: Human shouts scare best; habituation soon blunts effect
item.description: Research indicates that loud human noises and bright lights were effective in driving deer and elk away from crops, while predator sounds and dog barks didn’t have the same effect. Over a period of six weeks, these animals became accustomed to the deterrents, especially those near human activity. Researchers recommend diversifying stimuli and introducing consequences to keep these animals from adapting. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
